portici.intro: Portici's old trees live in the grounds of the Reggia, the royal palace on the Circumvesuviana line south of Naples. The upper park is now the botanical garden of the University of Naples Federico II, and Italy's national register picks out a ginkgo 22 metres tall, a camphor tree 4.2 metres round, an Australian Moreton Bay fig on buttress roots and a Canary pine. Down in the lower park, open only in part and with a guide, stands a downy oak 28 metres tall, the one native among them.
portici.meta_description: Old trees of the Reggia di Portici: a ginkgo, a wide camphor, a Moreton Bay fig, a Canary pine and a 28-metre downy oak in the royal park.
portici.question_meta: Which are the remarkable trees of Portici? Five trees in the Reggia's park, from a gold-turning ginkgo to a 28-metre downy oak.
portici.question_answer: The remarkable trees of Portici stand in the park of the Reggia. The widest is a camphor tree 420 centimetres round in the University's botanical garden, and the tallest is a downy oak of 28 metres in the lower park. A ginkgo, a Moreton Bay fig and a Canary pine are also on Italy's national register.
portici.question_context: All five trees grow in the grounds of the Reggia di Portici, but they make two different visits. The upper park holds the botanical garden of the University of Naples Federico II, which is ticketed, with hours that change by season. Inside it the ginkgo, number one on the register's Portici list, stands 22 metres tall and turns gold in November. About 75 metres from it the camphor tree has grown low and wide, 12 metres high on a trunk 420 centimetres round. On the east side, among palms and ferns, a Moreton Bay fig from eastern Australia stands on buttress roots next to two groups of Washingtonia palms. A Canary pine with long drooping needles is listed under the upper park but stands about 700 metres north-east of the garden, in a corner whose access we could not confirm. The lower park is only partly open and visited with a guide, and that is where the downy oak rises 28 metres, the only native species of the five. None of the five has a published age.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket to see the trees of Portici?
faq.a: Yes for four of them. The upper park is the University of Naples' botanical garden and charges entry, and the lower park, where the downy oak stands, is visited with a guide. Check hours with the Centro MUSA visitor centre before going.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit?
faq.a: November, when the ginkgo in the upper park turns gold. The other trees look much the same all year.

faq.q: How do I get to the Reggia di Portici?
faq.a: Take the Circumvesuviana from Naples to Portici-Via Libertà or Portici Bellavista, then walk about 10 minutes to the palace gate on Via Università.

faq.q: How old are the trees of Portici?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for any of them. If you know when one was planted, tell us.

castellammare-di-stabia.intro: Castellammare di Stabia has two old trees in a royal garden and a third that nobody can agree on. Up the hill, in the garden of the Reggia di Quisisana, the Campania region dates a great pine and a twisted yew to 1765, in the reign of Ferdinand IV, and both still stand by the King's first fountain. Down on the seafront, the Villa Comunale holds a towering araucaria that the national register calls a monkey puzzle and a 2022 photograph shows as a Norfolk Island pine.
castellammare-di-stabia.meta_description: Old trees of Castellammare di Stabia: a pine and a yew dated to 1765 in the Quisisana royal garden, and a disputed araucaria on the seafront.
castellammare-di-stabia.question_meta: What is the oldest tree in Castellammare di Stabia? A pine and a yew in the Quisisana garden, dated by the region to 1765.
castellammare-di-stabia.question_answer: The oldest trees in Castellammare di Stabia are a pine and a yew in the garden of the Reggia di Quisisana. The Campania region says both have stood there since 1765, making them roughly two and a half centuries old. The pine is the bigger, 495 centimetres round and 22 metres tall.
castellammare-di-stabia.question_context: The two oldest trees stand together by the King's first fountain in the historic garden of the Reggia di Quisisana, on the hill above the town. The Campania region dates both to 1765, in the reign of Ferdinand IV, king of Naples, and its dating is the only one there is. The pine is the largest of the garden, 495 centimetres round and 22 metres tall, though the region calls it an Aleppo pine while the national register lists the Calabrian variety. The yew is only 8 metres tall, with a twisted trunk and crown. Since 2020 the garden has belonged to the Parco archeologico di Pompei, and it is visited with the archaeological museum of Stabia in the palace, on a ticket. The third tree is free to see, in the Villa Comunale on the seafront, ten minutes from the station. Its species is disputed. The register says monkey puzzle, 30 metres tall, while a 2022 photograph shows the level, drooping tiers of a Norfolk Island pine of about 20 metres.

faq.q: Is the Quisisana garden open to visitors?
faq.a: Yes, on a ticket, as part of the Parco archeologico di Pompei together with the Stabia archaeological museum. Listings disagree on opening days and price, so check pompeiisites.org first.

faq.q: Is the araucaria in the Villa Comunale a monkey puzzle?
faq.a: Italy's national register says so, but a 2022 photograph shows a Norfolk Island pine, which fits its size better. We give both names. If you can settle it, tell us.

faq.q: How do I get to the trees?
faq.a: The Circumvesuviana stops at Castellammare di Stabia. The Villa Comunale is about 10 minutes on foot; Quisisana is a steep walk or a local bus up the hill.

monte-faito.intro: Monte Faito rises above Castellammare di Stabia and Vico Equense, and its beech forest once supplied the Sorrento peninsula with summer ice. At Pian del Pero, 1,167 metres up, four great beeches still line the old snow pits where winter snow was packed and stored. The Campania region presumes them about 400 years old, and the widest trunk is more than seven metres round. The trail starts free and ungated from a public road.
monte-faito.meta_description: Monte Faito's four beeches of Pian del Pero, presumed 400 years old, beside the old snow pits that sent ice to the Sorrento coast.
monte-faito.question_meta: What is the oldest tree on Monte Faito? Four beeches at Pian del Pero, presumed about 400 years old by the Campania region.
monte-faito.question_answer: The oldest trees on Monte Faito are four beeches at Pian del Pero, which the Campania region presumes to be about 400 years old. They stand within 15 metres of each other beside the old snow pits, with trunks of 450, 620, 680 and 705 centimetres round.
monte-faito.question_context: The four beeches of Pian del Pero stand at 1,167 metres in the beech forest of Monte Faito, in the Regional Park of the Monti Lattari. The Campania region describes them as four trees of about 400 years that lined the neviere, the snow pits where winter snow was packed and kept, then sent down to the Sorrento peninsula for the ice trade. The 400 years is the region's presumed age, not a ring count. The regional and national registers give trunks of 450, 620, 680 and 705 centimetres round and heights of 18 to 20 metres, and because they stand so close together we treat them as one place to stand. The path that starts there is the Sentiero dei Faggi Secolari e delle Antiche Neviere. The cable car from Castellammare di Stabia was the classic way up, but one travel guide reports it closed since April 2025 after a cable failure, so check before you go. Bus 009 from Vico Equense and the mountain road are the alternatives, and snow can close the road in winter.

faq.q: Is the Monte Faito cable car running?
faq.a: One travel guide reports it closed since April 2025 after a cable failure. Check with EAV before you go, or take bus 009 from Vico Equense or drive up the mountain road.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the beeches?
faq.a: Late October into November, when the beech wood turns copper. Snow can close the road in winter.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket?
faq.a: No. Pian del Pero is a trailhead on a public road with no gate.

sila.intro: The Sila plateau in Calabria holds two very different old-tree visits. Near Camigliatello Silano, I Giganti della Sila is a five-hectare reserve of Corsican pines, 58 of them estimated at more than 350 years old by the FAI, which runs it, and up to 43 metres tall; it is temporarily closed. In the Sila Piccola above Taverna, a free forest track from the Gariglione barracks passes a silver fir over five metres round and a 30-metre beech, both signed by the forest guards.
sila.meta_description: Sila's old trees: the Giganti della Sila pine grove, 350 years and up to 43 m (temporarily closed), and the signed fir and beech of Gariglione.
sila.question_meta: What are the oldest trees in the Sila? The Giganti della Sila, Corsican pines estimated at over 350 years, near Camigliatello Silano.
sila.question_answer: The oldest trees in the Sila are the Giganti della Sila, a grove of Corsican pines near Camigliatello Silano. The FAI estimates 58 of them at more than 350 years old, and the tallest reach 43 metres. The grove is temporarily closed by the FAI, with no reopening date announced.
sila.question_context: The two visits lie some distance apart on the plateau. I Giganti della Sila stands at about 1,400 metres near Croce di Magara, a few kilometres from Camigliatello Silano. The five hectares became the biogenetic nature reserve I Giganti di Fallistro by ministerial decree on 21 July 1987 and are now cared for by the FAI, the Italian heritage trust. Sources count between 52 and 60 pines, and the Sila National Park gives trunks of 2.5 to 6 metres round and heights of 30 to 43 metres. Visitors photographed the grove in August 2026, but the FAI has since closed it until further notice for extraordinary maintenance. The Gariglione trees, in the Sila Piccola above Taverna, are free to see. The silver fir stands beside the dirt track from the forest barracks towards the 1,759-metre summit, 515 centimetres round and 25 metres tall, and a beech 30 metres tall and 415 centimetres round stands about 170 metres further on. The forest guards put a sign at each, and a car is needed for both places.

faq.q: Is I Giganti della Sila open?
faq.a: Not at the moment. The FAI has closed the grove until further notice for extraordinary maintenance, with no reopening date announced. Check fondoambiente.it before going.

faq.q: Can I see old trees in the Sila while the Giganti are closed?
faq.a: Yes. The silver fir and the beech on the forest track from the Gariglione barracks above Taverna are free to visit and signed by the forest guards.

faq.q: When should I go to Gariglione?
faq.a: October, when the beech turns copper among the firs.

faq.q: Can I get there by public transport?
faq.a: We found none. Both places are reached by car, the grove from Camigliatello Silano and the Gariglione track from the forest barracks.

san-pietro-in-amantea.intro: San Pietro in Amantea is a small hill village inland from Amantea on Calabria's Tyrrhenian coast, and a tree stands at the heart of its main square. U Chiuppu, as the village calls it, is an oriental plane 32 metres tall and 467 centimetres round, listed on Italy's national register of monumental trees. It shares Piazza IV Novembre with a fountain from 1900 and the church of the Madonna delle Grazie, and it is free to see at any hour.
san-pietro-in-amantea.meta_description: U Chiuppu, the 32-metre oriental plane in the square of San Pietro in Amantea, Calabria, listed among Italy's monumental trees.
san-pietro-in-amantea.question_meta: What is the big tree in San Pietro in Amantea? U Chiuppu, an oriental plane 32 metres tall in Piazza IV Novembre.
san-pietro-in-amantea.question_answer: The big tree in San Pietro in Amantea is U Chiuppu, an oriental plane in Piazza IV Novembre. Italy's national register measures it at 32 metres tall and 467 centimetres round. It stands in the open square beside a fountain from 1900, free to see.
san-pietro-in-amantea.question_context: U Chiuppu stands in Piazza IV Novembre, which locals call Mmienzu U Largu, in the historic centre of San Pietro in Amantea. Italy's national register lists it as an oriental plane, 32 metres tall and 467 centimetres round, and a Calabrian travel site describes it as almost five metres round. The same square holds U Zutittu, a fountain from 1900, and the church of the Madonna delle Grazie, so the tree, the fountain and the church make one stop. Nobody has published when the plane was planted, and the most recent record we have found of it is a 2021 map entry, so a dated photograph from a visitor would help the next person who comes. The nearest railway station is Amantea, on the Tyrrhenian line, about four kilometres to the west as the crow flies. We could not confirm a bus link, so a car or taxi from Amantea is the simplest way up. There is no gate and no ticket, since the tree stands in the open village square.

faq.q: Where exactly is U Chiuppu?
faq.a: In Piazza IV Novembre, the main square of San Pietro in Amantea's historic centre, beside the fountain from 1900 and the church of the Madonna delle Grazie.

faq.q: How old is U Chiuppu?
faq.a: Nobody has published a planting date. If you know it, or the story behind the name, tell us.

faq.q: How do I get to San Pietro in Amantea?
faq.a: Take the train to Amantea on the Tyrrhenian line, then a car or taxi to the village, about four kilometres east as the crow flies.

serra-san-bruno.intro: Serra San Bruno, in the Serre mountains of Calabria, is known for its Carthusian monastery, and its most visited place is the sanctuary of Santa Maria del Bosco, a church among silver firs about two kilometres away. Italy's national register picks out one of those firs, 33 metres tall and 390 centimetres round, in the wood around the forecourt, Saint Bruno's small lake and the granite staircase. The sanctuary is free; the monastery itself is closed to visitors.
serra-san-bruno.meta_description: The monumental silver fir of Santa Maria del Bosco in Serra San Bruno, Calabria, 33 metres tall in the wood around the sanctuary.
serra-san-bruno.question_meta: What is the remarkable tree of Serra San Bruno? A 33-metre silver fir at the sanctuary of Santa Maria del Bosco.
serra-san-bruno.question_answer: The remarkable tree of Serra San Bruno is a silver fir at the sanctuary of Santa Maria del Bosco, listed on Italy's national register at 33 metres tall and 390 centimetres round. It stands in the fir wood around the forecourt, by Saint Bruno's lake and the granite staircase.
serra-san-bruno.question_context: Santa Maria del Bosco lies about two kilometres from the entrance of the Certosa, the Carthusian monastery of Serra San Bruno, and can be reached on foot or by car. The comune describes the sanctuary standing among secular silver firs and young beeches, with a large forecourt, the small lake of Saint Bruno and a granite staircase up to the church, and says tens of thousands of people visit in summer. The church is entered freely by its front staircase, though opening hours are not confirmed. The monastery itself is closed to visitors, but the sanctuary and its woods are not part of it. Italy's national register lists one fir here as monumental, 33 metres tall and 390 centimetres round, without describing the trunk, so the one to look for is the biggest fir around the forecourt. A fir was observed at that spot in 2021, and nothing more recent has been published. No source gives its age. If you visit and can say which fir it is, or how old it might be, tell us.

faq.q: Can I visit the Certosa of Serra San Bruno?
faq.a: The monastery itself is closed to visitors. The sanctuary of Santa Maria del Bosco and its fir wood, about two kilometres away, are open and free.

faq.q: How do I find the monumental fir?
faq.a: Look for the biggest silver fir around the sanctuary forecourt, by Saint Bruno's lake and the granite staircase. The register gives it 33 metres tall and 390 centimetres round.

faq.q: How do I get to Santa Maria del Bosco?
faq.a: Walk or drive about two kilometres from the Certosa entrance. There is no railway; Serra San Bruno has local buses.
